beats.text: In 1863, a woman led a military raid that freed more than 700 enslaved people in one night.

overlays.hook: In 1863, she led a raid that freed *more than 700* people in *one night.*

beats.text: She escaped slavery in 1849, then kept going back to free others.
In the Civil War, she worked as a Union scout and spy in South Carolina.

visual.caption: Union camp at Beaufort, South Carolina, 1861

beats.text: She recruited scouts to map the Combahee River,

visual.caption: The Combahee River on a Union Army map, 1865

beats.text: and learned where the Confederates had hidden mines.

visual.title: Hidden mines
visual.sub: laid in the river by the Confederates

beats.text: On the night of June 1, 1863, she guided Union gunboats up the river,
with about 300 soldiers, most of them Black.
Enslaved families ran and swam toward the boats.

visual.caption: Escaping to the boats, Harper's Weekly, 1863

beats.text: Soldiers burned plantations, rice mills and Confederate supplies.
By morning, more than 700 people were free.
Many of the freed men joined the Union Army.
In ten years on the Underground Railroad, she led about 70 people out. That night, ten times as many.
Yet she never got a soldier's pension, only a widow's.
One woman. One river. More than 700 lives.

facts.claim: In June 1863 Tubman led (with Col. James Montgomery) a Union raid on the Combahee River that freed more than 700 enslaved people, overnight June 1-2.
facts.note: Count: 'more than 700' (HOUSE, HIST), 'more than 750' (NPS). HOUSE: 'lead troops in a military operation'. Timing: night of June 1 to morning of June 2 (HIST, NPS).

facts.claim: Escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and returned repeatedly to guide others out.
Served the Union in South Carolina as a scout and spy.
Recruited scouts who gathered intelligence on the Combahee area.
facts.note: HIST: eight scouts helped her map the area.

facts.claim: The raid's intelligence located Confederate mines ('torpedoes') in the river.
On the night of June 1, 1863, Tubman guided Union gunboats (John Adams, Harriet A. Weed, Sentinel) up the Combahee.
About 300 soldiers: the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers (Black) plus about 50 from a Rhode Island unit.
Enslaved people ran and swam toward the gunboats.
Plantations, rice mills and supplies were burned.
More than 700 freed by the morning of June 2.
Many freed men enlisted in the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers.
About 70 people guided out over ten years on the Underground Railroad; 700+ in the raid (about ten times).
facts.note: Older figure of ~300 (Bradford 1868) is considered exaggerated (BRIT).

facts.claim: She was not paid a soldier's pension; she received a widow's pension (as Nelson Davis's widow, from 1892; raised to $20 in 1899).

notUsed: 'First woman to lead an armed raid in US history': stated in several places, but the US House site says 'first African-American woman to lead troops'; not used.
Tubman's description of women carrying babies, pigs and pots of rice (her own account via History.com): not used, one source.
Exact count (727 / 750 / 756 / 800): sources differ; script says 'more than 700'.
